facts.fact_text: The present case concerns the first applicant's static demonstration in November 2009.
The present case concerns the first applicant's prosecution for an administrative offence related to his static demonstration in November 2009.

The first applicant submitted a notice to the Gelendzhik municipality notifying them of his intention to hold a static demonstration on 26 November 2009 near the town office of the Federal Security Service (FSB).
The notice submitted by the first applicant to the Gelendzhik municipality specified that the event's goal was to draw the public's attention to the allegedly unlawful arrest of the second applicant.
On 26 November 2009 the first applicant held the demonstration as planned.
The present case concerns the first applicant's prosecution for an administrative offence related to his static demonstration in November 2009.

On 23 November 2009, referring to section 12 § 2 of the Public Events Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004) and Article 294 of the Criminal Code, the Gelendzhik municipality issued a warning document to the first applicant.
The warning document issued by the Gelendzhik municipality on 23 November 2009 invited the first applicant to abstain from holding the planned demonstration.
The warning document issued by the Gelendzhik municipality on 23 November 2009 indicated that if the demonstration were to be held, the first applicant and participants might be held liable.
By a judgment of 15 December 2009, a justice of the peace convicted the first applicant under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The justice of the peace sentenced the first applicant to a fine of 2,000 Russian roubles (approximately 45 euros at the time).

The justice of the peace held that the first applicant had committed a breach of public order on account of his failure to abstain from holding the demonstration despite the lawful warning document issued by the Gelendzhik municipality.
The justice of the peace stated that the first applicant's actions amounted to 'putting pressure on justice in relation to a specific criminal case'.
On 20 January 2010 the Gelendzhik Town Court of the Krasnodar Region upheld the judgment of 15 December 2009 convicting the first applicant.

The Gelendzhik Town Court of the Krasnodar Region stated that the goal of the first applicant's demonstration amounted to indirect interference with the administration of justice in the criminal case against Mr Ivanov.
By two decisions of 3 October 2011, an unspecified judge of Oktyabrskiy District Court of Novorossiysk authorised the tapping of the applicants' conversations on three mobile telephone numbers.
The authorisation for tapping the applicants' conversations on three mobile telephone numbers was granted from 3 October 2011 for 180 days.
By a judgment of 30 April 2013, the Town Court convicted the applicants as charged.
In its judgment of 30 April 2013, the Town Court held that the interception of the applicants' communications had been lawful and thus the records could be relied on as evidence.
In its judgment of 30 April 2013, the Town Court held that no circumstance was identified for rejecting the records of intercepted communications as inadmissible evidence.

In its judgment of 30 April 2013, the Town Court rejected the defendants' argument that the records of the intercepted telephone communications should not be used in evidence because during the preliminary investigation the investigator did not receive court decisions authorising the interception.

In its judgment of 30 April 2013, the Town Court rejected the defendants' argument that the records of the intercepted telephone communications should not be used in evidence because the court decisions did not bear the seal of the authorising court.
On 13 August 2013 the Krasnodar Regional Court upheld the judgment of 30 April 2013 convicting the applicants.

On 23 November 2009, referring to section 12 § 2 of the Public Events Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004) and Article 294 of the Criminal Code, the Gelendzhik municipality issued a warning document to the first applicant.

Pursuant to Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004 (the Public Events Act), a public event may be held in any convenient location, provided that it does not create a risk of building collapse or any other risks to the safety of the participants (section 8 § 1).

Under section 12 § 2 of Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004 (the Public Events Act), if the information contained in the notification or other factors give reason to believe that the aims of the public event or the manner of its conduct are contrary to the Constitution, the Criminal Code or the Code of Administrative Offences, the competent regional or municipal authority must warn the organisers in writing that they may be held liable for any unlawful actions, in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law.

For a summary of the relevant provisions of Federal Law no. 144-FZ of 12 August 1995 (the Operational-Search Activities Act), see Zubkov and Others v. Russia, nos. 29431/05 and 2 others, §§ 43-55, 7 November 2017.

Under section 9 of Federal Law no. 144-FZ of 12 August 1995 (the Operational-Search Activities Act), a court decision authorising an operational-search activity (such as the interception of telephone communications) must be certified with a seal and handed over to the requesting authority.

Under section 9 of Federal Law no. 144-FZ of 12 August 1995 (the Operational-Search Activities Act), the administration of the courts must ensure the protection of the data contained in the documents submitted by the requesting authority.

Under section 12 of Federal Law no. 144-FZ of 12 August 1995 (the Operational-Search Activities Act), a court decision authorising an operational-search activity and the material submitted for making such an order are both kept only by the authority carrying out the operational-search activity.

According to the Constitutional Court of Russia, in decision no. 460-O-O of 15 July 2008 (unpublished), operational-search activities results may be used in evidence in criminal proceedings only after a court decision authorising the operational-search activity or a copy of such a decision has been admitted to the criminal case file.

According to the Constitutional Court of Russia, in decision no. 1585-O-O of 17 November 2011 (unpublished), section 12 of Federal Law no. 144-FZ of 12 August 1995 (the Operational-Search Activities Act) did not prohibit the defendant having access to the court decision or receiving a copy of the court decision authorising an operational-search activity, and thus did not impede the right to seek judicial review of such a court decision.
The two documents submitted by the prosecutor during the trial did not bear the name of the authorising judge or the official seal of the authorising court.
The photocopies of the decisions of 3 October 2011 submitted by the FSB on 27 November 2012 had not been signed by a judge and did not bear the official seal of the authorising court.
The photocopies of the decisions of 3 October 2011 submitted by the FSB on 27 November 2012 bore the seal of the FSB office.

On 27 July 2015 the Judiciary Department of the Supreme Court of Russia informed the second applicant that pursuant to paragraph 12.5 of the Instruction on case processing in a district court (adopted by the Judiciary Department of the Supreme Court of Russia in its Decree no. 36 of 29 April 2003), copies of court decisions issued by a court must be certified with the signature of the judge presiding in the relevant case.

The Judiciary Department of the Supreme Court of Russia informed the second applicant on 27 July 2015 that if certification by the presiding judge is not possible, copies of court decisions must be certified by the signature of the (deputy) president of the court or another authorised member of personnel, such as a court clerk.
The Judiciary Department of the Supreme Court of Russia informed the second applicant on 27 July 2015 that copies of court decisions must bear the official seal of the court.

The Judiciary Department of the Supreme Court of Russia informed the second applicant on 27 July 2015 that in order to certify compliance of the copy with the original court decision, it must be stamped 'Copy verified' and the court's seal must appear on the last sheet of the court decision.

On 24 August 2015 the FSB's regional office gave a reply similar to that of the Judiciary Department of the Supreme Court of Russia, concluding that the FSB's regional office had no authority to certify copies of court decisions.
On 13 July 2016 the FSB's regional office informed one of the applicants' co-defendants that the originals of court decisions nos. 706 and 707 of 3 October 2011 had been kept in file no. 543.

The FSB's regional office informed one of the applicants' co-defendants on 13 July 2016 that in October 2013 file no. 543 had been disposed of, as it no longer had any practical, scientific or historical value.

During the trial, the prosecutor submitted two documents that appeared to be excerpts from the decisions of 3 October 2011 authorising the tapping of the applicants' telephone communications.
The two documents submitted by the prosecutor during the trial did not bear the name of the authorising judge or the official seal of the authorising court.

At a court hearing on 27 November 2012 the prosecutor requested the trial court to require the FSB to submit the decisions of 3 October 2011 authorising the tapping of the applicants' telephone communications.
On 27 November 2012 the FSB submitted photocopies of the decisions of 3 October 2011 authorising the tapping of the applicants' telephone communications.
The photocopies of the decisions of 3 October 2011 submitted by the FSB on 27 November 2012 had not been signed by a judge and did not bear the official seal of the authorising court.
The photocopies of the decisions of 3 October 2011 submitted by the FSB on 27 November 2012 bore the seal of the FSB office.

The Town Court noted in its judgment of 30 April 2013 that authorities carrying out operational-search activities rely on the Operational-Search Activities Act and the Instruction of 17 April 2007 on providing the operational-search activities results to an enquirer, an investigator, a prosecutor or a court.

The Town Court noted in its judgment of 30 April 2013 that under section 13 of the Instruction of 17 April 2007, operational-search activities results arising from the interception of telephone communications should be accompanied by a copy of the related court decisions authorising the operational-search activities.
On 27 November 2012 the trial court admitted to the file copies of court decisions nos. 706 and 707 dated 3 October 2011 authorising the tapping of the applicants' telephone communications.
The Town Court noted in its judgment of 30 April 2013 that an authorised official certified the copies of court decisions nos. 706 and 707 and apposed an appropriate seal.

The Town Court held in its judgment of 30 April 2013 that the court decisions were requested and admitted to the file in compliance with Articles 271 and 286 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, section 11 of the Operational-Search Activities Act and paragraphs 11 and 21 of the Instruction of 17 April 2007.

The Town Court held in its judgment of 30 April 2013 that the fact that court decisions nos. 706 and 707 were not handed over to the investigator during the investigation does not tarnish the operational-search activities results.
On 13 August 2013 the Krasnodar Regional Court upheld the judgment of 30 April 2013 convicting the applicants.

In February 2013 the FSB informed the second applicant that, pursuant to section 5 of the Operational-Search Activities Act, the second applicant had not at that time acquired the right to have access to the information received in the framework of file no. 543.

The FSB informed the second applicant in February 2013 that he had not acquired the right to access information in file no. 543 because he was not a person whose guilt had not been established in the relevant procedure (by way of a refusal to institute criminal proceedings or to discontinue such proceedings for lack of evidence that a crime had been committed or corpus delicti).

The FSB informed the second applicant in February 2013 that within the measures taken for the purposes of file no. 543, the FSB received information indicating that the second applicant, Mr Achilov, and two others had committed crimes under Article 159 of the Criminal Code.

The FSB informed the second applicant in February 2013 that the relevant material from file no. 543 was transferred to the investigating authority in order to take a decision on whether or not to institute criminal proceedings.
The FSB informed the second applicant in February 2013 that criminal proceedings were instituted on 21 February 2012.

The FSB informed the second applicant in February 2013 that it had no other information indicating that the second applicant had committed other offences, for instance under Article 282.1 of the Criminal Code.
